steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our LeBenchmark 2.0 paper, an updated framework for self-supervised speech representations of French. It should motivate SSL for speech, explain why standardized benchmarking is needed, and summarize what the new version adds.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- SSL success across domains and in speech processing
- Need for fair comparison and standardized evaluation of speech SSL
- Existing benchmarks (SUPERB and its extensions) and their limits
- LeBenchmark 2.0: what it provides and the paper's contributions

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- SSL success
  - pretext tasks from massive unlabeled data
  - domains: audio/speech/language (cite), computer vision (cite), robotics (cite), embedded devices and sensors (cite), medicine (cite)
  - speech: almost every sub-field impacted by large pre-trained SSL models
  - SOTA reported for ASR, AER, ASV, AST, SLU, SE, SS (cite each)
  - also useful for under-resourced languages: A. Babu et al., H. Nguyen et al. (cite); accessibility across many languages
- Need for standardization
  - fair comparisons, standardized protocols to assess value of new architectures
  - NLP early adopter: GLUE, SuperGLUE (cite)
- Existing benchmarks
  - SUPERB (cite): first English-only suite, 13 tasks on well-known datasets, common fine-tuning protocol
  - limit: no standardized pre-training / hyperparameters; models on hundreds of thousands of hours next to few hundred hours or other languages
  - extensions: SUPERB-SG generative tasks e.g. speech enhancement (cite); ML-SUPERB multilingual (cite); Indicsuperb Indian languages (cite); SLUE for SLU (cite)
  - LeBenchmark (cite): French, freezes pre-training data and fine-tuning procedure; released pre-trained models incl. largest/best French SSL
  - otherwise: arbitrary, heterogeneous comparisons (data, protocols, hyperparameter tuning); resources scarce; need rigorous, fair, replicable protocol
- LeBenchmark 2.0
  - first version (cite), definition of D. Schlangen (cite): foundations for comparing SSL on French downstream tasks
  - language-specific SSL outperforms multilingual depending on downstream conditions (cite + this work)
  - 2.0: standardized, fully replicable, extended framework
  - pre-training set up to fourteen thousand hours of French speech (Section 3)
  - three new SSL models, thirty million to one billion parameters (Section 4)
  - two new tasks: ASV and syntactic analysis of spoken French (Section 5)
  - discussion: energy footprint (Section 6), language-specific vs language-agnostic pre-training (Section 5)
  - collective attempt to unify French SSL community: common models, datasets, protocols

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Self-Supervised Learning (SSL) solves pretext tasks that are extracted automatically from massive unlabeled data, and deep learning systems powered by SSL now give groundbreaking performance in a lot of domains, including audio, speech and language processing, computer vision, robotics, embedded devices and sensors, and medicine. In speech processing specifically, almost every sub-field has been largely impacted by the large pre-trained SSL models that became available. Impressive improvements and state-of-the-art performance on competitive datasets were reported for Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR), Automatic Emotion Recognition (AER), Automatic Speaker Verification (ASV), Automatic Speech Translation (AST), Spoken Language Understanding (SLU), Speech Enhancement (SE), Speech Separation (SS), and many other tasks. Most leaderboards are built around English, but SSL was also shown to be very useful for under-resourced languages, as previous studies demonstrated, and this greatly increases access to cutting-edge speech technologies in many languages.

Of course, with SSL for speech growing so fast, we need fair comparisons and standardized evaluation protocols that properly assess what each new architecture adds. Other domains adopted this earlier, for instance Natural Language Processing (NLP) with the GLUE and SuperGLUE benchmarks, and then a first English-only evaluation suite appeared for speech, SUPERB. SUPERB bundles 13 different tasks based on well-known datasets to benchmark new SSL models with a common fine-tuning evaluation protocol. But SUPERB does not standardize the pre-training process and hyperparameters, so models trained on hundreds of thousands of hours of speech are in the same leaderboard as models trained with a few hundred hours or even on different languages. SUPERB was extended to generative tasks like speech enhancement with the same standardized protocol in SUPERB-SG, and to multiple languages in ML-SUPERB, and it was specialised to Indian languages in Indicsuperb. There are also benchmarks targeting one specific task, such as SLUE for SLU. LeBenchmark looked at SSL benchmarking in French from a unified perspective by freezing both the available pre-training data and the fine-tuning procedure. It also released a set of pre-trained SSL models to the community, including the largest and best-performing French SSL systems. Apart from these two attempts, most SSL models are compared in an arbitrary and heterogeneous way, with different pre-training and fine-tuning datasets, evaluation protocols and hyperparameter tuning. Standardization and resources for SSL evaluation are still scarce, and it is crucial that the community puts more effort in these directions, because the scientific value of a released model can only be validated against a rigorous, fair and replicable evaluation protocol.

- LeBenchmark 2.0
  - first version, definition of D. Schlangen: foundations for comparing SSL on French downstream tasks
  - language-specific SSL outperforms multilingual depending on downstream conditions (previous work + this work)
  - 2.0: standardized, fully replicable, extended framework
  - pre-training set up to fourteen thousand hours of heterogeneous French speech (Section 3)
  - three new SSL models, thirty million to one billion parameters (Section 4)
  - two new tasks: ASV and syntactic analysis of spoken French (Section 5)
  - discussion: energy footprint (Section 6), language-specific vs language-agnostic pre-training (Section 5)
  - collective attempt to unify French SSL community: common models, datasets, protocols

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Self-Supervised Learning (SSL) solves pretext tasks that are extracted automatically from massive unlabeled data, and deep learning systems powered by SSL now give groundbreaking performance in a lot of domains, including audio, speech and language processing, computer vision, robotics, embedded devices and sensors, and medicine. In speech processing specifically, almost every sub-field has been largely impacted by the large pre-trained SSL models that became available. Impressive improvements and state-of-the-art performance on competitive datasets were reported for Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR), Automatic Emotion Recognition (AER), Automatic Speaker Verification (ASV), Automatic Speech Translation (AST), Spoken Language Understanding (SLU), Speech Enhancement (SE), Speech Separation (SS), and many other tasks. Most leaderboards are built around English, but SSL was also shown to be very useful for under-resourced languages, as previous studies demonstrated, and this greatly increases access to cutting-edge speech technologies in many languages.

Of course, with SSL for speech growing so fast, we need fair comparisons and standardized evaluation protocols that properly assess what each new architecture adds. Other domains adopted this earlier, for instance Natural Language Processing (NLP) with the GLUE and SuperGLUE benchmarks, and then a first English-only evaluation suite appeared for speech, SUPERB. SUPERB bundles 13 different tasks based on well-known datasets to benchmark new SSL models with a common fine-tuning evaluation protocol. But SUPERB does not standardize the pre-training process and hyperparameters, so models trained on hundreds of thousands of hours of speech are in the same leaderboard as models trained with a few hundred hours or even on different languages. SUPERB was extended to generative tasks like speech enhancement with the same standardized protocol in SUPERB-SG, and to multiple languages in ML-SUPERB, and it was specialised to Indian languages in Indicsuperb. There are also benchmarks targeting one specific task, such as SLUE for SLU. LeBenchmark looked at SSL benchmarking in French from a unified perspective by freezing both the available pre-training data and the fine-tuning procedure. It also released a set of pre-trained SSL models to the community, including the largest and best-performing French SSL systems. Apart from these two attempts, most SSL models are compared in an arbitrary and heterogeneous way, with different pre-training and fine-tuning datasets, evaluation protocols and hyperparameter tuning. Standardization and resources for SSL evaluation are still scarce, and it is crucial that the community puts more effort in these directions, because the scientific value of a released model can only be validated against a rigorous, fair and replicable evaluation protocol.

In the first version of LeBenchmark, following the definition of D. Schlangen, we wanted to provide the necessary foundations to investigate and compare SSL models on French downstream tasks. Language-specific SSL clearly outperforms multilingual models depending on the downstream conditions, as shown in our previous work and in the present work. LeBenchmark 2.0 builds on this to provide a standardized, fully replicable and extended framework for assessing and developing SSL representations of French speech. In particular, we release a well-curated pre-training set with up to fourteen thousand hours of heterogeneous French speech (Section 3), three new pre-trained SSL models from thirty million to one billion parameters (Section 4), and two new evaluation tasks, for ASV and for syntactic analysis of spoken French (Section 5). LeBenchmark 2.0 also discusses the energy footprint of SSL models (Section 6) and the difference between language-specific and language-agnostic pre-training (Section 5). To sum up, LeBenchmark 2.0 is a collective attempt to unify the French SSL community around common models, datasets and evaluation protocols.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Through solving pretext tasks automatically extracted from massive unlabeled data, Self-Supervised Learning (SSL) powered deep learning systems deliver groundbreaking performance across a wide range of domains including audio, speech, and language processing [1,2,3], computer vision [4,5], robotics [6], embedded devices and sensors [7], and medicine [8,9]. In the specific context of speech processing, almost every sub-field has been largely impacted by newly available large pre-trained SSL models. Indeed, impressive improvements and state-of-the-art performance on competitive datasets have been reported for Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) [10,11,12], Automatic Emotion Recognition (AER) [13,14,15], Automatic Speaker Verification (ASV) [16,17,15], Automatic Speech Translation (AST) [18,19], Spoken Language Understanding (SLU) [15,20,21,22], Speech Enhancement (SE) [23,24,25], Speech Separation (SS) [23,26], and many others. Although most leaderboards are built around the English language, SSL has also been reported to be remarkably useful for under-resourced languages, as demonstrated by A. Babu et al. [19] and H. Nguyen et al. [18], greatly increasing the accessibility of cutting-edge speech technologies across many languages.

Naturally, the flourishing field of SSL for speech calls for fair comparisons and standardized evaluation protocols that properly assess the added value of each newly introduced architecture. Following other early-adopter domains such as Natural Language Processing (NLP) with, for instance, the GLUE [27] and SuperGLUE benchmarks [28], a first English-only evaluation suite appeared: SUPERB [15]. In SUPERB, 13 different tasks based on well-known datasets are bundled together to benchmark novel SSL models following a common fine-tuning evaluation protocol. However, SUPERB does not standardize the pre-training process and hyperparameters, and models trained on hundreds of thousands of hours of speech appear in the same leaderboard as those learned with a few hundred hours or even on different languages. SUPERB has been extended to generative tasks such as speech enhancement, following the same standardized evaluation protocol, in SUPERB-SG [26], as well as to multiple languages in ML-SUPERB [29], or specialised to Indian languages with Indicsuperb [30]. Other benchmarks targeting a specific task, such as SLUE for SLU [31], have also been proposed. LeBenchmark approached SSL benchmarking in French from a unified perspective by freezing the available pre-training data as well as the fine-tuning procedure [32,14]. It also introduced a set of pre-trained SSL models available to the community, including the largest and best-performing French SSL systems. Aside from these two attempts, most SSL models are currently compared in an arbitrary and heterogeneous fashion across different pre-training and fine-tuning datasets, evaluation protocols, and hyperparameter tuning. Standardization and resources for SSL evaluation remain scarce, and it is crucial for the community that further efforts are made in these directions. Indeed, the scientific value of a released model can only be validated against a rigorous, fair and replicable evaluation protocol.

With the first version of LeBenchmark [32,14], and following the definition of D. Schlangen [33], we aimed to provide the necessary foundations for investigating and comparing SSL models on French downstream tasks. Indeed, language-specific SSL, as shown in [32,14] and in the present work, clearly outperforms multilingual models depending on the downstream conditions. LeBenchmark 2.0 builds on this to provide a standardized, fully replicable, and extended framework for the assessment and development of SSL representations of French speech. In particular, we release a well-curated pre-training set containing up to fourteen thousand hours of heterogeneous French speech (Section 3), three novel pre-trained SSL models ranging from thirty million to one billion parameters (Section 4), and two new evaluation tasks for ASV and syntactic analysis of spoken French (Section 5). LeBenchmark 2.0 also broadens the discussion to the energy footprint of SSL models (Section 6) and the difference between language-specific and language-agnostic pre-training (Section 5). In short, LeBenchmark 2.0 is a collective attempt to unify the community of SSL for the French language around common models, datasets and evaluation protocols.
